title: Why Michigan Got the Upper Peninsula: The Toledo War
summary: A 1787 line drawn from maps that put Lake Michigan too far north left Ohio and Michigan both claiming the 468-square-mile Toledo Strip. Congress gave the strip to Ohio and paid Michigan with most of the Upper Peninsula, a prize Michigan first voted down.
tags: why does michigan have the upper peninsula
sources: Northwest Ordinance, 13 Jul 1787, Article 5: Congress may form one or two States 'north of an east and west line drawn through the southerly bend or extreme of Lake Michigan' (Avalon Project, Yale Law School): https://avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/nworder.asp

Michigan Dept. of Military and Veterans Affairs, The Toledo War: the 1787 line from the southern tip of Lake Michigan; maps showed it meeting Lake Erie north of the Maumee River; William Harris survey (1817) and John A. Fulton survey; the strip 'a total of 468 square miles', 8 miles apart at Lake Erie and 5 at the Indiana border; Gov. Stevens T. Mason; Gov. Robert Lucas turned the region into a county named after himself; Ohio budget $300,000, Michigan $315,000; Michigan militia captured nine surveyors; Two Stickney stabbed a Michigan sheriff in a tavern brawl; Michigan gained 'the western three-quarters of the upper peninsula as compensation', '9,000 square miles of the most valuable timber, iron, and copper country in America': https://www.michigan.gov/dmva/about/history/military-events/highlights/the-toledo-war

Michigan State University, Geography of Michigan, The Toledo War: maps showed Lake Michigan 'much farther north than it actually is'; Harris (1817) ran the Ohio constitution's line, not due east; Fulton (1818) ran the ordinance line due east, leaving the Maumee's outlet in Michigan; strip of 468 square miles; Ohio had two senators and nineteen representatives, Michigan one non-voting delegate; no one was killed; Ohioan Two Stickney stabbed a Michigan sheriff; signed by President Jackson on June 15; the Detroit Free Press called the Upper Peninsula 'a region of perpetual snows'; opponents dubbed the second convention the 'Frostbitten Convention'; the Upper Peninsula rich in lumber, copper and iron ore: https://project.geo.msu.edu/geogmich/toledo_war.html

Michigan Legislature, Michigan Manual 2021-2022, pp. 20-21: in compensation Congress offered 9,000 square miles in what is now the Upper Peninsula; the first convention at Ann Arbor (26-30 Sep 1836) rejected the compromise 28-21; the second ('Frost-Bitten') convention met at Ann Arbor on 14-15 Dec 1836 and assented; Act of June 15, 1836 (5 Stat. 49): https://www.legislature.mi.gov/documents/2021-2022/michiganmanual/2021-MM-P0020-P0021.pdf

An act to admit the State of Michigan into the Union (5 Stat. 144): recites the Act of June 15, 1836 establishing the northern boundary of Ohio and the convention's assent of 15 Dec 1836: https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/5/144
Derived: 9,000 / 468 = about 19 times the land (from the Michigan Manual and DMVA figures above)

Map data: Natural Earth (public domain) https://www.naturalearthdata.com and US Census Bureau cartographic boundary files (public domain) https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/carto-boundary-file.html; the 1787, Harris, Fulton and 'old maps' lines and the strip are drawn schematically

scenes.narration: Michigan once went to war with Ohio, and lost. Its prize for losing was this.
The Upper Peninsula: about {9,000|nine thousand} square miles that Michigan said it didn't want.
So why is this piece of Michigan attached to Wisconsin? It started with a bad map, and a fight over one city: Toledo.
Both states called out their militias. And when Congress offered a deal, Michigan voted it down.
By the end, you'll know how one bad line started a war, and why Michigan may have won by losing.

scenes.chapter: A line from a bad map
scenes.narration: In {1787|seventeen eighty-seven}, the Northwest Ordinance drew a line due east from the southern tip of Lake Michigan.
But the maps of the day put Lake Michigan too far north. On paper, the line met Lake Erie above the {Maumee|maw-mee} River.
The real tip is farther south. Run the line due east from there, and the river's mouth, where Toledo stands, falls on Michigan's side.
Ohio wanted that river mouth. In {1817|eighteen seventeen}, surveyor William Harris ran a line slanting north, to keep it in Ohio.

data.source: Michigan State University, Geography of Michigan

scenes.narration: A year later, John Fulton ran it due east, the way the Ordinance said.
Between the two lines: the Toledo Strip. {468|Four hundred sixty-eight} square miles, with Toledo inside.
If you like maps that explain things, subscribe. There's a new map every other day.
Michigan wanted to become a state, strip and all. Its young governor, Stevens T. Mason, would not let it go.
Ohio's governor, Robert Lucas, made the strip a county, and named it after himself.
Ohio set aside {$300,000|three hundred thousand dollars} for the fight. Michigan: {$315,000|three hundred and fifteen thousand}.
Michigan's militia even captured {nine|nine} surveyors.
And the death toll? Zero. No one was killed.
What did happen: in a tavern brawl, an Ohioan named Two Stickney stabbed a Michigan sheriff. Yes, his name was Two.
In Congress, it wasn't close. Ohio had {2|two} senators and {19|nineteen} representatives. Michigan, not yet a state, had one delegate, with no vote.

data.title: Ohio had the *votes*
data.source: Michigan State University, Geography of Michigan

scenes.narration: On {June 15, 1836|June fifteenth, eighteen thirty-six}, President Jackson signed the deal. Ohio gets the strip. Michigan can be a state, if it agrees.
And in exchange: about {9,000|nine thousand} square miles up north, most of the Upper Peninsula.
Michigan was not grateful. One Detroit paper called it a region of perpetual snows.
In September {1836|eighteen thirty-six}, a Michigan convention voted the deal down, {28|twenty-eight} to {21|twenty-one}.
So in December, a second convention met in Ann Arbor, and said yes. Opponents mocked it as the Frostbitten Convention.
In {1837|eighteen thirty-seven}, Michigan became the {26th|twenty-sixth} state: with the Upper Peninsula, and without Toledo.
And that region of perpetual snows? Michigan's own history pages call it the most valuable timber, iron and copper country in America.
Ohio got Toledo. Michigan got about nineteen times the land, the prize it tried to turn down.
So yes: Michigan lost a war to Ohio. Its prize for losing is still on every map.
There's a new map every other day. Pick one, and I'll see you there.
